messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia Haddad is a 38-year-old divorced school principal who came to treatment carrying herself with the controlled vigilance of someone who does not expect any place to stay safe for long. Before she could settle into the therapist’s office, she noted the door, the second exit through the adjoining reception area, and the windows. She said she always does this now, needing to know how she would get out before she can pay attention to anything else. Even at home she moves through her house this way, checking locks, noticing sightlines, listening for sounds in the yard, feeling on guard in rooms that used to feel ordinary.

Her trauma occurred during combat deployment several years earlier. Nadia does not tell the story in a smooth sequence. When she tries, the account breaks apart and she becomes frustrated, saying she knows the pieces are there but cannot put them in the right order. She remembers being in a convoy and then, in the next breath, being outside the vehicle; she is unsure what came first, the blast or the shouting. What is most immediate is not a clear timeline but sound. When the memory comes back, she hears it again in her head: the violent crack, metal striking metal, someone yelling commands, someone else screaming. Those sounds arrive with such force that for a moment they seem closer than the room she is actually in. She also remembers the hot surge of anger that followed—anger at the attack, at the chaos, at people around her, at how exposed and breakable everyone suddenly was. Even now, when the memory surfaces, rage is what rises fastest, sharp enough that she has to clench her jaw and grip the arms of her chair.

In the months after she returned home, Nadia found that the world no longer arranged itself into safe and unsafe places in any predictable way. The combat zone had made total sense to her in one respect: danger was real, vigilance was useful, and trust could be costly. Back in the United States, she had expected to resume civilian life, but she found herself unable to relax into it. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, not strangers and not even people who presented themselves as helpful. She watched others carefully for inconsistency, hidden motives, carelessness. In meetings at school she sat where she could see the door and scanned the room while teachers were talking. At assemblies she found herself calculating where students would be moved if something happened and which hallway would clear fastest. These habits fit easily enough with some parts of being a principal—being responsible, being prepared—but for Nadia they were not just professional diligence. They were the only way she could feel barely comfortable.

Her daily work repeatedly brushes against what happened to her. Sudden noises in a school building—the bang of a heavy door, a dropped stack of books over the intercom static, children shouting down a hallway—can make her body tense before she has time to think. On those days the auditory fragments of the deployment return, and with them fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame, all felt intensely and often all at once. She is ashamed of how quickly she reacts internally and of how much effort it takes to appear composed in front of staff and students. She has come to see these reactions as proof that she is, in her words, “a lousy coper,” someone who should have been able to handle what happened better and should certainly be able to live normally by now.

Over time this belief has narrowed her life. At work she keeps interactions efficient and guarded, delegating more than she used to and avoiding the kind of informal trust-building with teachers and parents that the role once required naturally of her. At home, being alone has not brought relief; it has simply meant there is no one else to share the burden of watching. After her divorce, the house became even quieter, but not more peaceful. She moves through it alert, checking routes out, unable to feel fully off duty. What troubles her almost as much as the fear is the deadened sense that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore. She still does what needs to be done and is regarded as competent, but the work that once mattered to her deeply now often feels hollow, as if she is performing the outline of a life rather than living one.

She sought help after recognizing how little of herself remained available to her work and relationships. A recent incident at school, when a loud crash in the hallway instantly filled her head with the sounds of the convoy attack, left her shaken and furious for hours, long after the building had settled. What finally frightened her was not only the intensity of the reaction but the thought that this might be all her life would ever be: scanning exits, mistrusting people, and moving through days that no longer feel meaningful. What she hopes for is modest but urgent—to be in a room, at school or at home, without first planning how to escape it, and to believe that her reactions do not define her as weak.
